Adak and the Unangax̂

Indigenous history of Adaax in the central Aleutian Islands

Adak Island is part of the ancestral homeland of the Unangax̂ people, also known as Aleut. In the Unangam Tunuu language, the island’s name is Adaax. Its coast preserves evidence of more than six millennia of human history. Russian-era records show that people still lived on Adak in 1827, shortly before the island’s permanent Native settlements ended. Repatriation assessments identify a cultural affiliation between Adak’s ancestors and the Native Village of Atka. [3] [13] [15] [19]

NameMeaning
Adak Island or AdaaxAn ancestral Unangax̂ homeland in the Andreanof Islands, between the Bering Sea and the North Pacific. [3] [11]
City of AdakA municipality on Kuluk Bay that incorporated in 2001 after the former military base closed. [5] [1] [2]
Native Village of AtkaA federally recognized Unangax̂ tribal government based on Atka Island, about 90 air miles east of Adak. [10] [6]

The first known settlements

A midden near Clam Lagoon contains shells, animal remains and traces of human activity. Alaska’s Office of History and Archaeology places early occupation on Adak at roughly 6,500 years ago. Research published in The People Before puts the earliest Clam Lagoon deposit near 7,000 calendar years ago. Dates depend in part on the sample and how researchers calibrate it. Shells and marine bones can yield older apparent ages than land-based material from the same deposit, so researchers measured the local offset. The date of first arrival remains open. [13] [9] [29] [12] [14]

Stone tools point to links across the island chain. Researchers identified Okmok volcano on Umnak Island as the most likely known source of obsidian found on Adak. The volcanic glass had traveled hundreds of miles. The objects show that material moved between islands, although the route and the people who carried it remain unknown. [12] [29]

Later deposits tell different stories. At Zeto Point, ancient DNA identified bones of young Aleutian cackling geese that were too young to fly. The finding shows that the geese once bred on Adak. Shells at Sweeper Cove tell another story of repeated coastal use, with dated deposits spanning parts of the eighth through nineteenth centuries. [30] [9]

Life on the islands

Food homes and sea travel

Adak’s Unangax̂ forebears used both sheltered shorelines and open water. Island records and excavations document fishing and the use of shellfish, seabirds and marine mammals. The wider Unangax̂ region relied on a seasonal mix of salmon, marine fish and game. Working together to harvest and process food and sharing the catch helped families through lean periods. [11] [9] [12] [8]

Partly underground houses used earth and sod for shelter. Driftwood and, in some cases, whale bones held up roofs. Across the region, people crossed rough water in lightweight skin-covered kayaks called iqyax and used larger open boats for carrying passengers and cargo. People used animal hides for boat coverings and sewed gut into rainwear. The same marine resources therefore supplied food, clothing and transportation. [11] [8] [23]

Language and oral history

Unangam Tunuu has several historically documented dialects. The Western or Atkan variety belongs to the central Aleutians, where Atka is a living center of the language. The name Unangax̂ refers to a person. The western plural is Unangas and the eastern plural is Unangan. Atka speakers William Dirks Sr. and Moses Dirks worked with linguist Knut Bergsland on writing and teaching materials. Moses Dirks also coauthored How the Atkans Talk with Anna Berge. [6] [8] [4]

Cedor L. Snigaroff’s Atkan Historical Traditions preserves accounts he told in 1952. It is a named Indigenous source for the central Aleutians. The published record leaves many Adak village names and island-specific stories uncertain. Atka materials carry their own place and speaker histories. [26] [29]

Art music and spiritual life

Fine grass basketry and bentwood hunting hats are documented Unangax̂ arts. In Atka, educator Crystal Dushkin researched drum rhythms, words and movements and helped create songs and dances for the Atka Dancers. These works show how families teach language and history through performance. [23] [25] [7]

The Aleutian Pribilof Islands Association describes regional traditions in which spiritual specialists used song, dance and drumming. Some feasts remembered the dead and distributed food and goods. Russian Orthodoxy took hold during the colonial period. Unangax̂ speakers helped develop written materials, and the priest Jacob Netsvetov arrived on Atka in 1829. St. Nicholas Russian Orthodox Church remains part of Atka’s community life. [8] [4] [24] [6]

Colonial rule and wartime removal

The Russian fur trade

Russian expeditions reached the Aleutian region in the 1740s. The sea otter fur trade depended on Indigenous hunters and their knowledge of the sea. Russian traders used force to secure labor. Historian Roza Lyapunova describes a Russian crew that entered Adak’s harbor around 1770 and took hostages to secure hunting operations. Her account records opposition on Adak. Across the Aleutians, violence, forced labor and imported disease upended villages. [8] [15]

An 1827 Russian-American Company count preserved in K. T. Khlebnikov’s records listed 193 Unangax̂ people on Adak. That was an island count. Khlebnikov recorded moves from Adak and Amlia toward the company settlement on Atka. The City of Adak also describes forced moves to Kodiak, the Pribilof Islands and Sitka. These sources record different routes and leave many individual family histories unresolved. [15] [11]

Permanent Unangax̂ villages on Adak ceased to be occupied around 1830. Seasonal hunting and fishing continued into the twentieth century. The United States acquired Russia’s claim to Alaska in 1867. Adak was included in the Aleutian Islands National Wildlife Refuge in 1913. [11] [18]

War on Adak and displacement from Atka

In 1942, the United States built a base on Adak for the campaign against Japanese forces on Attu and Kiska. The Alaska Native civilian community in this part of the story was on Atka. U.S. authorities removed 83 Atka residents and burned their village to prevent Japanese forces from using it. Authorities took the residents to an old herring plant at Killisnoo, near Angoon in Southeast Alaska. Seventeen died during the stay. Survivors returned in 1945, and the Navy helped rebuild the village. Some Attu survivors, who had been held in Japan, also settled on Atka. [20] [6] [17] [21]

Atka survivor Alice Petrivelli’s testimony appears in the National Park Service’s study of Killisnoo. Unangax̂ elder Barbara Shangin later gathered family and community accounts for Dear Ancestors and Descendants, a booklet about her parents’ wartime removal. In 1988, Congress enacted restitution for eligible Unangax̂ survivors and communities affected by the federal relocation. [17] [16] [28]

Adak today

The city and ancestral lands

The Navy’s military mission on Adak ended in 1997. The City of Adak incorporated in 2001. Congress ratified a land exchange in 2002, and the Aleut Corporation, an Alaska Native regional corporation, received about 47,000 acres on Adak in 2004. That transfer included the port and much of the former developed base. The federal wildlife refuge includes designated wilderness on the island’s southern portion. [2] [1] [27] [11]

Repatriation and Atka

In a 2018 case covering five Andreanof Islands, the Smithsonian’s National Museum of Natural History identified ancestral remains and funerary objects from Adak and other islands as culturally affiliated with the Native Village of Atka. A 2025 federal notice concerning ancestors from several islands, including Adak, identified the same tribal connection. The January 2026 federal list recognizes the Native Village of Atka and has no separate listing for an Adak tribe. [19] [22] [10]

Chronology

DateEvent
About 6,500–7,000 years agoThe Clam Lagoon deposits preserve traces of early settlement. [13] [29]
Mid to late 1700sRussian fur traders reach the central Aleutians and use coercion on Adak. [15]
1827 to the 1830sA company count records 193 Unangax̂ on Adak. Permanent Native villages cease to be occupied in the following years. [15] [11]
1867 and 1913The United States acquires Alaska. Adak later becomes part of a federal wildlife refuge. [18] [11]
1942–1945Adak becomes a U.S. base. U.S. authorities force Atka residents to Killisnoo. Survivors return in 1945. [20] [17]
1988Congress enacts restitution for qualifying survivors and communities. [28]
1997–2004The military mission ends, Adak incorporates and a land exchange transfers about 47,000 acres to the Aleut Corporation. [2] [1] [27]
2018 and 2025Smithsonian and federal records identify the Native Village of Atka’s cultural affiliation with ancestors from Adak. [19] [22]

Historical maps and geography

1875 map of Alaska’s Native peoples. William H. Dall’s map includes an Aleutian inset. It shows how a nineteenth-century U.S. surveyor grouped peoples after decades of colonial displacement.

1942 map of the landing at Adak. The Harry S. Truman Library preserves this annotated wartime map of the August 30 landing. The sheet records military use of the island.

1957 Adak topographic quadrangle. The U.S. Geological Survey sheet shows the coast, bays and elevations at 1:250,000 scale.

Indigenous Peoples and Languages of Alaska. The Alaska Native Language Archive map depicts language regions and traditional territories at approximately 1900.

Adak and Atka in the central Aleutians. The Alaska Division of Geological & Geophysical Surveys report locates both islands in Figure 1. It also links to separate maps of the modern communities.

Adak Island land status. U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service map AKM-067 shows present-day land categories, including designated wilderness and private lands.
